sandhi.note: तस्य + आपततः → तस्यापततः (a + ā → ā). The -aḥ of आपततः before the vowel e becomes y, which is dropped, leaving the gap आपतत एव; एव + आशु → एवाशु (a + ā → ā).
The visarga of सः is dropped before any consonant.
Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra.

samasa.sense: keen-edged (the final ā of धारा is shortened in the masculine bahuvrīhi)

morph.note: Present participle आपतत् (आ + √पत् + शतृ), genitive singular, agreeing with तस्य: ‘of him (as he was) rushing on’. The genitive belongs to गदाम् — his mace was cut while he was still in mid-charge.
Perfect ātmanepada of सम् + आ + √दा: reduplicated द-दे (the root’s ā is lost before the ending -ए). Verbs of taking with आ commonly take the middle: ‘took up for himself’.

mantras.anvaya: तस्य आपततः एव (सतः) गदां चण्डिका शितधारेण खड्गेन आशु चिच्छेद। सः च शूलं समाददे।
mantras.anvaya_en: First sentence: subject चण्डिका, object गदाम् (with its possessor तस्य आपततः), instrument खड्गेन शितधारेण, verb चिच्छेद. Second: सः … शूलं समाददे.
mantras.lit: Even as he was rushing on, Caṇḍikā swiftly cut his mace with her sharp-edged sword; and he took up a spear.
mantras.tr: Before he could reach her, Caṇḍikā’s keen sword had cut through his mace; and he snatched up a spear.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Before he could reach her’ renders the participle with एव, ‘even while rushing on’.

comm.t: The mace is destroyed before it can be used. Niśumbha changes weapons once more; the spear he now takes is the weapon of his last charge.

samasa.literal: he in whose hand is a spear

samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (अर्दन, agent noun in -अन from √अर्द् ‘to torment’)
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, अमराणाम् अर्दनः; the sense is the same.

samasa.sense: driven home with all her speed

morph.note: Perfect of √व्यध्: in the reduplicated syllable the semivowel य becomes इ (samprasāraṇa), giving वि-व्याध, with vṛddhi of the root vowel.
आविद्ध is the past participle of आ + √व्यध् with samprasāraṇa (व्यध् → विध्): ‘hurled, flung’.
Present participle of सम् + आ + √या, accusative singular masculine (stem समायान्त्-): ‘as he came on’.

mantras.anvaya: चण्डिका शूलहस्तं समायान्तम् अमरार्दनं निशुम्भं वेगाविद्धेन शूलेन हृदि विव्याध।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (चण्डिका), object (निशुम्भम् with three epithets), instrument (शूलेन वेगाविद्धेन), place (हृदि), verb (विव्याध).
mantras.lit: Caṇḍikā pierced in the heart Niśumbha, the tormentor of the immortals, as he came on spear in hand, with a spear hurled with force.
mantras.tr: As Niśumbha, scourge of the gods, came at her spear in hand, Caṇḍikā drove her spear with all her force into his heart.

comm.t: The decisive blow: spear against spear, and hers reaches his heart first. शूल, ‘spear’ or ‘trident’, is the Goddess’s own weapon in this battle (9.15, 9.28).
The epithet अमरार्दन, ‘tormentor of the immortals’, is placed at the moment of his fall: the cause of the gods’ suffering since chapter 5 is now ended by her hand.

sandhi.type: consonant sandhi (t before n), then visarga sandhi
sandhi.note: Final t becomes the nasal n before the nasal n (optional, but usual). Then -aḥ before a becomes -o and the a is absorbed (avagraha): निःसृतोऽपरः.
-aḥ before the voiced m becomes -o; visarga before t becomes s; तिष्ठ + इति → तिष्ठेति (a + i → e).

morph.note: Past participle of निस् + √सृ ‘to go out’. Verbs of motion form an active क्त participle, which here is the only verb of the sentence: ‘(another) came forth’.
Past passive participle of √भिद् ‘to split, pierce’: द + त → न्न (भिन्न). In the genitive with तस्य: ‘of him, pierced by the spear’.
Present participle of √वद् (stem वदत्), nominative singular masculine वदन्: ‘saying’. It carries the quoted तिष्ठ.

mantras.anvaya: शूलेन भिन्नस्य तस्य हृदयात् महाबलः महावीर्यः अपरः पुरुषः ‘तिष्ठ’ इति वदन् निःसृतः।
mantras.anvaya_en: No finite verb: the participle निःसृतः is the predicate. Subject पुरुषः with अपरः, महाबलः, महावीर्यः and वदन्; source हृदयात् with the genitive phrase भिन्नस्य तस्य शूलेन.
mantras.lit: From the heart of him, pierced by the spear, came forth another being, of great strength, of great valour, saying ‘Stop!’
mantras.tr: Out of his pierced heart came another being, mighty and valiant, crying, ‘Stop!’

comm.t: A strange moment: from Niśumbha’s pierced heart a second figure (अपरः पुरुषः) emerges, still defiant, and shouts the battle-cry ‘Stop!’ that the Goddess had used against Śumbha (9.24). The text does not explain who or what he is.

One traditional reading takes the figure as Niśumbha’s own life or inner strength leaving the body, still bent on battle; the Goddess must cut that down too before he is truly dead. The verse itself says only ‘another man, of great strength’.
A modern reading: what drove Niśumbha does not die with the first wound. It must be met where it comes out of the heart.

flags.uncertain: The identity of the अपरः पुरुषः is not stated; the reading as Niśumbha’s inner self is interpretation, offered as such.

sandhi.note: The final t stays unvoiced before the unvoiced t; the words are written together.
Visarga before c becomes s, then palatal ś.
ततः + असौ → ततोऽसौ (avagraha); असौ + अपतत् → असावपतत् (au → āv before a vowel); अपतत् + भुवि → अपतद्भुवि (t voiced to d before bh).

morph.note: Present participle of निस् + √क्रम्, genitive singular. √क्रम् lengthens its vowel in the parasmaipada present (क्रामति), so the participle is क्रामत्; निस् becomes निष् before k. ‘Of him (as he was) going out’ — the figure of 9.35.

A possessive adjective स्वनवत् ‘having sound, resounding’ in the neuter accusative, used as an adverb: ‘laughing aloud’. The -वत् of comparison (‘like a sound’) is possible in form but makes poor sense here.
Nominative singular masculine of the pronoun अदस् ‘that, yonder one’, often used for a person just mentioned: ‘he’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः देवी स्वनवत् प्रहस्य निष्क्रामतः तस्य शिरः खड्गेन चिच्छेद। ततः असौ भुवि अपतत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: First sentence: subject देवी, absolutive phrase स्वनवत् प्रहस्य, object शिरः with the genitive तस्य निष्क्रामतः, instrument खड्गेन, verb चिच्छेद. Second: असौ भुवि अपतत्.
mantras.lit: Then the Goddess, laughing aloud, cut off with her sword the head of him who was coming out; thereupon he fell to the ground.
mantras.tr: Then the Goddess laughed aloud and with her sword struck off the head of the one who was coming forth, and he fell to the earth.

comm.t: The Goddess beheads the figure that came out of Niśumbha’s heart, laughing as she does it, and ‘he’ falls. This is the death of Niśumbha that gives the chapter its name (निशुम्भवधः); in 10.2 Śumbha sees his brother slain.

The Goddess’s laughter at the moment of slaying recurs in the text (as with Mahiṣa, whose final form she also strikes as it emerges). Her calm and her laughter mark the battle as play (līlā) for her, not struggle.

flags.uncertain: असौ (‘he’) may refer to the emerging figure or to Niśumbha; the two are not distinguished by the text, and 10.2 treats Niśumbha as slain.

samasa.vigraha: दंष्ट्राभिः क्षुण्णाः शिरोधराः येषां ते, तान्
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (containing दंष्ट्राक्षुण्ण, a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa: दंष्ट्राभिः क्षुण्णाः)
samasa.literal: those whose necks are crushed by fangs
samasa.sense: the asuras whose necks the lion had crushed in its jaws

morph.note: Perfect of √खाद्: reduplicated syllable च (kh → c), root unchanged in the 3rd singular: चखाद. One verb serves three subjects — the lion, Kālī, Śivadūtī.
Neuter accusative of the adjective उग्र used as an adverb (‘fiercely’); it cannot agree with any noun of the verse.

mantras.anvaya: ततः सिंहः दंष्ट्राक्षुण्णशिरोधरान् तान् असुरान् उग्रं चखाद। तथा काली (चखाद), तथा शिवदूती अपरान् (चखाद)।
mantras.anvaya_en: One verb (चखाद) with the lion as its expressed subject; Kālī and Śivadūtī are added with तथा, and अपरान् gives them their own victims.
mantras.lit: Then the lion fiercely devoured those asuras whose necks were crushed by its fangs; likewise Kālī, likewise Śivadūtī (devoured) others.
mantras.tr: Then the lion savagely devoured the asuras, crushing their necks in its jaws, and Kālī and Śivadūtī devoured others in the same way.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Crushing their necks in its jaws’ renders the compound adjective as an action.

comm.t: With Niśumbha dead, the rout of his army begins. The lion, Kālī and Śivadūtī devour the asuras — the three who are named together again in 9.41.
Kālī (Cāmuṇḍā) and Śivadūtī both devour asuras elsewhere in the uttama carita (Kālī in 7.8–10 and the Raktabīja battle, Śivadūtī in 8.38); devouring is their particular way of ending the enemy.
